nodes.label: Service before Faction
nodes.description: Professional service can offer a common standard where factions compete for influence. Its credibility depends on institutions that reward competence rather than loyalty alone.

nodes.label: Security Directorate
nodes.description: A security directorate offers the council a firmer grip on opposition and administration. It also threatens the independent knowledge on which sound policy depends.

nodes.label: Officer Standards
nodes.description: Officer standards should demand preparation as well as obedience. More professional training requires time that cannot also be spent on immediate expansion.

nodes.label: Screen the Cadres
nodes.description: Screening the civil service can remove rivals but also deprive the state of experience. Recovery will suffer if political suspicion becomes a substitute for administration.

nodes.label: Civilian Nationalists
nodes.description: Civilian nationalists can supply expertise and a connection to political traditions outside the officer corps. Bringing them in will make the council's decisions more contested.

nodes.label: Defence Industry First
nodes.description: Defence industry can support the council's promise of security. Farms and the civilian economy will bear the opportunity cost of that priority.

nodes.label: Civil Recovery First
nodes.description: Civil recovery offers a different basis for military legitimacy. Put reconstruction ahead of a rapid expansion in weapons production.

nodes.label: A Military Workshop
nodes.description: A dispersed military workshop can provide a more reliable repair and production base. Its construction must still be supported by the resources of the economy.

nodes.label: Public Works and Peace
nodes.description: Demobilisation can return labour to civilian life and make public works possible. It also reduces the manpower held ready for military service.

nodes.label: Audit Military Firms
nodes.description: Military enterprises should not be exempt from public accounting. Auditing them will challenge interests close to the council itself.

nodes.label: A Permanent Council
nodes.description: A permanent council would turn emergency authority into a governing institution. It must accept the long term political and intellectual costs of that choice.

nodes.label: Civilian Transition
nodes.description: A civilian transition needs a process that the armed forces cannot quietly reverse. Set the terms of a handover through negotiations with credible civilian representatives.

nodes.label: Armed Neutrality
nodes.description: Armed neutrality promises to defend sovereignty without another patron's direction. Maintaining that posture can narrow the resources available for development.

nodes.label: Constituent Assembly
nodes.description: A constituent assembly can give the next civil order a public foundation. Its disagreements are part of the transition rather than proof that transition has failed.

nodes.label: A Regular Mandate
nodes.description: The provisional mandate must either become a defined institution or give way to a civilian order. End the uncertainty over who is entitled to govern and under which rules.

nodes.label: Survey the War Economy
nodes.description: Bomb damage, dispersed workshops and interrupted transport make a reliable economic survey essential. Establish which productive facilities can be restored and where the most urgent bottlenecks lie.
nodes.available_code: COLDWAR_VIE_is_1970 = yes

nodes.label: Disperse Workshops
nodes.description: Dispersed workshops are harder to neutralise in one attack. They also sacrifice some of the efficiency of production concentrated around a common infrastructure.

nodes.label: Restore the Centres
nodes.description: Industrial centres can bring labour, power and transport back into closer coordination. Concentration creates its own vulnerabilities and demands reliable supply.

nodes.label: Mobile Repair Crews
nodes.description: Mobile crews can repair links that fixed offices are too slow to reach. Their labour must be drawn from other pressing tasks in the civilian economy.

nodes.label: Haiphong Power
nodes.description: Haiphong's productive role depends on usable power as well as access to the sea. Prepare the rehabilitation and construction needed to restore that foundation.

nodes.label: Reconnect the North
nodes.description: Northern districts cannot recover in isolation from one another. Reconnect the transport links on which production, food distribution and administration depend.

nodes.label: Capital Goods First
nodes.description: Capital goods promise a stronger productive base in the future. Giving them priority asks households to carry a heavier burden in the present.

nodes.label: Civilian Needs First
nodes.description: Recovery must deliver goods that households need now. Place civilian consumption ahead of some demands for rapid military industrial expansion.

nodes.label: Northeastern Industry
nodes.description: The northeastern economy needs a wider range of industrial capacity. Organise a construction project capable of supporting later production rather than another paper target.

nodes.label: Hanoi Workshops
nodes.description: Hanoi's workshops can serve the needs of a recovering civilian economy. Prepare their expansion within the limits of available construction and capital.

nodes.label: A Technical Workforce
nodes.description: Skilled workers and technicians are as necessary as machinery. Fund the training that allows restored facilities to produce reliably.

nodes.label: Domestic Components
nodes.description: Domestic components can make essential production less vulnerable to an interrupted import. Their development may require accepting a slower rise in efficiency.

nodes.label: Specialist Machinery
nodes.description: Specialist machinery can relieve constraints that domestic workshops cannot yet overcome. Access to it brings both opportunities and greater exposure to international conditions.

nodes.label: A Repair Depot
nodes.description: A repair depot can keep scarce equipment useful for longer. Its organisation requires staff, stocks and common technical standards.

nodes.label: Engineering Contracts
nodes.description: Engineering contracts can bring knowledge that is difficult to acquire alone. Negotiate practical assistance without assuming that an invitation guarantees a partner.

nodes.label: An Industrial Recovery
nodes.description: Recovery has become more than the immediate repair of wartime damage. Consolidate the productive base while recognising the costs that a long conflict has left behind.

nodes.label: Secure the Rice Supply
nodes.description: Food supply is a daily test of national resilience. Review procurement and distribution before a poor harvest or a broken transport link becomes a wider emergency.
nodes.available_code: COLDWAR_VIE_is_1970 = yes

nodes.label: Raise Procurement
nodes.description: Higher collective procurement targets can make deliveries to the state more predictable. They can also weaken incentives where households retain too little of their additional effort.

nodes.label: Expand Plot Incentives
nodes.description: Household plots already have a place beside collective farming. Expand their incentives and productive role rather than treating every useful local practice as a deviation.

nodes.label: Irrigation Crews
nodes.description: Irrigation work can make organised rural labour more productive. Prepare a district project that improves the agricultural base rather than merely increasing procurement demands.

nodes.label: Village Market Access
nodes.description: Village producers need a practical route to buyers and supplies. Improve market access while maintaining the administrative work that makes exchange possible.

nodes.label: A Grain Reserve
nodes.description: A grain reserve can cushion distribution when ordinary deliveries fail. Keeping it useful requires supervision, storage and a willingness to bear its cost.

nodes.label: Fertiliser and Tools
nodes.description: Fertiliser and machinery can improve the return on rural labour. Import dependence and the cost of inputs remain part of that calculation.

nodes.label: Labour for the Land
nodes.description: Land improvement can be organised around the labour available within the country. Those crews cannot simultaneously rebuild roads, factories and housing.

nodes.label: Northern Rice Districts
nodes.description: Strengthen northern rice production through a new agricultural district. The project must be planned and built before its capacity can be relied upon.

nodes.label: Dykes and Local Roads
nodes.description: Dykes and local roads protect the connection between the harvest and the population it must feed. Their maintenance is less spectacular than a new industrial target, but no less necessary.

nodes.label: Health and Nutrition
nodes.description: Health and nutrition determine whether rural households can sustain their work. Extend practical provision while recognising its recurring demands on the state.

nodes.label: Universal Rations
nodes.description: Universal rations can preserve a measure of security through an uncertain recovery. They require the budget and distribution service to continue supporting the guarantee.

nodes.label: Farm Contracts
nodes.description: Procurement contracts can give producers a clearer connection between obligations and reward. Their incentives change the authority exercised by local officials.

nodes.label: Rural Distribution
nodes.description: A rural distribution service can bring essential goods closer to the people producing the harvest. Its reliability depends on resources as well as instructions.

nodes.label: Market the Surplus
nodes.description: A marketable surplus can improve the prospects of rural producers. The resulting trade also exposes them more directly to changing economic conditions.

nodes.label: Food Security
nodes.description: Food security has improved through stronger production and distribution. Some expense and inefficiency will remain even after the worst shortages have been relieved.

nodes.label: Review the People’s War
nodes.description: The People's Army has accumulated experience under exceptional conditions. Review what that experience can teach without assuming that endurance removes the need for organisation and resources.
nodes.available_code: COLDWAR_VIE_is_1970 = yes

nodes.label: Local Defence
nodes.description: Local defence can use knowledge of terrain and dispersed organisation. It offers a different priority from concentrating resources in a larger military industrial effort.

nodes.label: Combined Arms
nodes.description: Combined arms operations require coordination among forces with different demands. Their effectiveness depends on a supply system able to sustain the concentration.

nodes.label: Redundant Supply Lines
nodes.description: A redundant network can keep supplies moving when one route fails. Building and maintaining it diverts resources from civil construction.

nodes.label: A General Staff
nodes.description: A professional general staff must turn experience into reliable planning. More demanding preparation will take longer than rapid mobilisation alone.

nodes.label: Defend Hanoi
nodes.description: Hanoi and Haiphong require a more coherent air defence network. Prepare additional defensive installations without assuming that hardware can replace trained crews and organisation.

nodes.label: An Affordable Army
nodes.description: An affordable army must be matched to the resources the country can sustain. Reduce its demands even where that means holding fewer people ready for service.

nodes.label: Mobilisation Reserves
nodes.description: Large mobilisation reserves preserve a capacity for prolonged war. Farms and rural households must live with the labour those reserves absorb.

nodes.label: Repair before Replace
nodes.description: Repair can keep scarce military equipment in use. Concentrating on existing systems also limits the resources available to investigate new ones.

nodes.label: Train Reserve Cadres
nodes.description: Reserve cadres need training that can be repeated and passed on. The programme consumes time and labour that civilian reconstruction also requires.

nodes.label: Coastal Approaches
nodes.description: The coastal approaches connect military security to trade and everyday supply. Organise a sustainable patrol programme suited to the country's resources.

nodes.label: Coastal Defence
nodes.description: Coastal defence offers practical protection before expensive naval prestige. Such concentration reinforces a more guarded relationship with the outside world.

nodes.label: Small Fleet Repairs
nodes.description: A small fleet needs repair capacity before it can remain reliably at sea. Prepare a dockyard project that the country can sustain.

nodes.label: Civil Defence Teams
nodes.description: Civil defence and medical teams protect the ability of communities to endure disruption. Their work also requires a continuing social commitment.

nodes.label: Aircrew Training
nodes.description: A sustainable air force begins with trained crews and instructors. Give education and maintenance knowledge a place beside demands for additional aircraft.

nodes.label: The Service Settlement
nodes.description: Peace allows service personnel to return to civilian work and family life. Their settlement requires support, and demobilisation relinquishes part of the wartime recruitment advantage.

nodes.label: The Divided Nation
nodes.description: North and South remain separate political orders in a country whose future is contested. Military action, negotiation and the responsibilities of eventual peace must all be considered.
nodes.available_code: COLDWAR_VIE_is_1970 = yes

nodes.label: Pressure at the Front
nodes.description: Pressure at the front can improve the position from which terms are discussed. It also concentrates forces and places heavier demands on supply.

nodes.label: The Paris Talks
nodes.description: The Paris talks offer a channel in which opponents can test one another's terms. Negotiation will require work and concessions without guaranteeing national reunification.

nodes.label: Southern Corridors
nodes.description: The southern corridors must remain usable if military pressure is to be sustained. Their protection competes with the rebuilding of the civil economy.

nodes.label: Terms and Guarantees
nodes.description: Terms and guarantees have value only where the other parties are prepared to accept them. Exchange proposals while preserving a clear account of the responsibilities each government would assume.

nodes.label: After the Fighting
nodes.description: The end of large scale fighting will not itself create a functioning civil settlement. Prepare the administrative and social work that must follow it.

nodes.label: Unified Administration
nodes.description: Where the southern states are actually under our administration, a common framework can begin. Joining institutions after a long war will produce disruption before it produces coherence.

nodes.label: Peaceful Coexistence
nodes.description: Peaceful coexistence would preserve two administrations while reducing the danger of renewed war. Such a settlement asks both governments to accept limits on their immediate objectives.

nodes.label: Southern Recovery
nodes.description: Southern recovery requires knowledge of existing production and distribution. Rebuilding should preserve what works while confronting the dislocation of national integration.

nodes.label: Families across Borders
nodes.description: Families should not remain indefinitely separated by the political division. Organise channels of contact without pretending that trust can be restored by decree.

nodes.label: Citizens First
nodes.description: Citizenship must offer a future beyond permanent wartime labels. A sustainable civil order needs practical protection for people whose past does not fit one political narrative.

nodes.label: Political Screening
nodes.description: Security led screening places political control ahead of an open return to civil life. Exclusion and displacement will slow recovery and create further social obligations.

nodes.label: Conditional Amnesty
nodes.description: Conditional amnesty can bring former opponents back into productive and public life. The political leadership must accept the uncertainty that genuine reconciliation entails.

nodes.label: A Civil Register
nodes.description: A common civil register can reduce administrative confusion. It must not conceal the insecurity created where people remain excluded from the settlement.

nodes.label: Resettle the Displaced
nodes.description: Displaced people and veterans need a route to stable homes and livelihoods. Resettlement is a public responsibility with costs that cannot be wished away.

nodes.label: A Sustainable Peace
nodes.description: A sustainable peace is measured by the society it permits to recover. Consolidate the settlement without treating military mobilisation as a permanent source of political purpose.

nodes.label: Two Patrons
nodes.description: Chinese and Soviet assistance make possible an effort beyond the means of the domestic economy. Their rivalry gives Vietnam room to manoeuvre and reasons to guard its independence.
nodes.available_code: COLDWAR_VIE_is_1970 = yes

nodes.label: The Soviet Relationship
nodes.description: A deeper Soviet relationship can bring specialist knowledge and a more dependable channel of cooperation. It also ties national planning more closely to one outside partner.

nodes.label: Balance the Patrons
nodes.description: Balancing Moscow and Beijing can preserve diplomatic room for manoeuvre. It requires careful administration of relationships whose priorities do not always coincide.

nodes.label: Soviet Specialists
nodes.description: Soviet specialists can assist with problems that domestic institutions cannot yet solve alone. Their invitation requires agreement and practical preparation on both sides.

nodes.label: Strategic Autonomy
nodes.description: Vietnamese objectives cannot simply be delegated to either patron. Defend strategic autonomy even where it limits easier access to outside support.

nodes.label: Laos and Cambodia
nodes.description: Events in Laos and Cambodia affect security, supply and the prospects for peace. Maintain channels through which their governments can answer proposals in their own right.

nodes.label: Regional Commitments
nodes.description: Regional commitments can strengthen military cooperation while extending the burden on supply. Their terms must be accepted rather than presumed.

nodes.label: Regional Restraint
nodes.description: Restraint and withdrawal can reduce the demands of regional confrontation. They also require the leadership to temper expectations built around military pressure.

nodes.label: Defend the Border
nodes.description: Northern defence must remain credible even during reconstruction. Preparing the frontier does not decide whether another government will choose confrontation.

nodes.label: Build Regional Trust
nodes.description: Confidence building can make regional restraint more durable. It requires continuing diplomatic work rather than a declaration that old disputes have vanished.

nodes.label: Trade under Isolation
nodes.description: Diplomatic isolation need not end every form of trade. Develop practical resilience while acknowledging the friction imposed by restricted access and uncertain partners.

nodes.label: Strategic Self Reliance
nodes.description: Strategic self reliance can reduce vulnerability to pressure from outside. It may also mean accepting slower progress where domestic capabilities remain limited.

nodes.label: A Controlled Opening
nodes.description: A controlled opening can connect the economy to a wider range of opportunities. The country will also experience more of the world's economic fluctuations.

nodes.label: Diversify Suppliers
nodes.description: Alternative suppliers can reduce the risk created by one interrupted relationship. Maintaining those connections brings its own costs of coordination.

nodes.label: Earlier Normalisation
nodes.description: Earlier normalisation would require the other governments to accept a different diplomatic course. Begin the negotiations without assuming that their sanctions or security policies have already changed.

nodes.label: After the Bloc Crisis
nodes.description: The socialist world is changing, and established support cannot be assumed indefinitely. Prepare the institutions and relationships through which Vietnam can adapt.

nodes.label: The Long War
nodes.description: The long war has bound local political cadres, village networks and regular formations into a single struggle. Preserve that experience as the army prepares for the campaigns still ahead.

nodes.label: Political Liaison
nodes.description: Maintain contact with local institutions and southern allies. Communist revolutionary support is distinct from the general army programme.

nodes.label: Small Unit Schools
nodes.description: Teach a regular army to operate in a dispersed war without treating militias as free equipment or manpower.

nodes.label: Local Organization
nodes.description: Rely on local initiative and political contact while accepting that decentralized command complicates major offensives.

nodes.label: Regional Staffs
nodes.description: Connect dispersed formations to a functioning staff and replacement system. The extra organization requires administrators.

nodes.label: Army and Movement
nodes.description: Coordinate local political organization and the regular army. Both preparatory lines must be completed.

nodes.label: Dispersed Warfare
nodes.description: Make territorial defence and endurance the priority. This is useful during invasion, but gives up planning depth for a decisive offensive.

nodes.label: Main Force War
nodes.description: Concentrate the regular army for a prepared campaign. Supply demand rises and formations become harder to sustain.

nodes.label: A War of Endurance
nodes.description: Improve the army’s ability to preserve a territorial defence. The policy is not a damage bonus for an imaginary underground army.

nodes.label: Prepared Operations
nodes.description: Prepare the regular army for the current campaign, whether against South Vietnam or an invading force. Southern revolutionary support remains a separate optional action.

nodes.label: Review the Campaign
nodes.description: Turn the actual campaign experience into a doctrine lesson. A failed offensive does not receive a fabricated victory.

nodes.label: Local Guarantees
nodes.description: Use land adjudication, representation and civilian guarantees to address political grievances. FULRO is a conditional highland problem, not a label for all minorities.

nodes.label: Security First
nodes.description: Make intensive internal security deployment the first response. It offers organization while prolonging administrative and civilian burdens.

nodes.label: Services and Land
nodes.description: Fund schools, local administration and a credible land settlement. Services take resources before they yield political benefits.

nodes.label: Security Screening
nodes.description: Keep a forceful security programme under periodic review. More deployment does not remove the social causes of resistance.

nodes.label: A Political Settlement
nodes.description: Review the chosen local policy with representation from the affected population. Security and civilian guarantees remain distinct choices.

nodes.label: Keep the Reserve
nodes.description: Retain a trained reserve for renewed danger. Civilian recovery continues to lose labour to defence.

nodes.label: Return to Civil Life
nodes.description: Reduce the exceptional military commitment and direct labour towards production. Readiness grows more slowly.

nodes.label: A Rotating Reserve
nodes.description: Make retained readiness more sustainable through rotation. The reserve still carries an economic cost.

nodes.label: Veterans in Civil Life
nodes.description: Support demobilized veterans and affected households. Productive recovery requires sustained public spending.

nodes.label: Record the Lessons
nodes.description: Preserve the doctrinal lessons without maintaining every temporary wartime measure indefinitely.

nodes.label: Beyond the Long War
nodes.description: Conclude a programme of military learning and political recovery. Renewed war can reopen funded operational decisions without paying focus rewards twice.

nodes.label: The Cambodian Question
nodes.description: Keep Cambodia’s sovereignty and changing political situation distinct from Vietnam’s own war. Cambodia is not an inevitable starting enemy.

nodes.label: Protect the Frontier
nodes.description: Prepare a defined defensive plan for the southwestern frontier. Military preparation draws resources from reconstruction.

nodes.label: Protect Border Civilians
nodes.description: Organize relief and temporary administration for threatened communities. Protection requires public spending.

nodes.label: Southwestern Command
nodes.description: Unify the existing border staff and maintain a limited commitment. This is not an automatic invasion order.

nodes.label: Mekong Logistics
nodes.description: Prepare the transport and administrative base for a real southwestern campaign. Keep relief and military logistics functioning without waiting for the opponent to agree to talks.

nodes.label: Define the War Aim
nodes.description: Choose whether to limit the commitment or pursue the overthrow of a hostile government. Existing Cambodian cooperation remains an alternative.

nodes.label: Keep the War Limited
nodes.description: Limit the military objective to protection of the frontier. It preserves resources but may leave a hostile regime in place.

nodes.label: End Hostile Rule
nodes.description: Authorize a regime change war aim against a hostile Cambodian government. The war aim is not a completed victory or puppet state.

nodes.label: A Monitored Border
nodes.description: Seek a verified frontier arrangement and a lower military commitment. Refusal leaves the conflict unresolved.

nodes.label: Phnom Penh Objective
nodes.description: Prepare an operation towards the enemy capital. Taking it must be achieved through normal combat and begins a new political problem.

nodes.label: Secure the Victory
nodes.description: Convert an actually won campaign into a strategic result. End the hostile border threat, record hard military lessons and open the route to a durable Cambodian security partner.

nodes.label: A Friendly Cambodia
nodes.description: Build a durable strategic buffer after a real victory. A friendly Cambodian security partner lets Vietnam recover the southwest while retaining a credible regional position.

nodes.label: Direct Military Rule
nodes.description: Take a heavier direct security role in occupied territory. Immediate control increases the long term burden on Vietnam.

nodes.label: Train the Partner
nodes.description: Fund Cambodian military responsibility through native assistance. A trained partner reduces the verified Vietnamese commitment and makes victory sustainable rather than an endless occupation.

nodes.label: Dry Season Operations
nodes.description: Conduct a defined campaign against armed opposition where the real war or occupation system can represent it. Military pressure is not automatic reconciliation.

nodes.label: The Long Commitment
nodes.description: Account for the garrisons, advisers and civilian costs that follow intervention. A capital victory is not an endless national bonus.

nodes.label: Stay and Secure
nodes.description: Retain a larger commitment while pursuing greater security. The northern frontier and civilian recovery compete for the same resources.

nodes.label: Prepare to Leave
nodes.description: Negotiate a reduction of the Vietnamese commitment and arrangements for the partner government. Withdrawal does not mean Cambodian civil war has ended.

nodes.label: Rebuild Occupied Land
nodes.description: Use the actual MD state investment system for occupied non core recovery. Its cash contribution, political cost and project limits remain real.

nodes.label: Verify the Drawdown
nodes.description: Check actual troops, military access and the agreed commitments before declaring withdrawal complete. A focus never teleports armies.

nodes.label: A Regional Process
nodes.description: Seek a wider political process with distinct Cambodian actors. Talks with noncommunist opposition are not recognition of Khmer Rouge crimes.

nodes.label: Southwestern Security
nodes.description: Keep the strategic gains of the chosen outcome. A defeated threat and a friendly Cambodian partner can support a continuing security dividend; limited frontier agreements receive no military victory reward.

nodes.label: The Northern Frontier
nodes.description: Treat China as an important neighbour whose cooperation and rivalry can both shape Vietnam’s security. A later war is conditional.

nodes.label: A Border Commission
nodes.description: Propose a serious boundary channel while retaining sovereignty. China must agree before a bilateral commission exists.

nodes.label: Survey the Defences
nodes.description: Survey defensive positions and prepare local fieldworks. Better knowledge of the ground helps existing formations entrench; it does not construct free forts.

nodes.label: Protect Civil Rights
nodes.description: Keep citizenship and property treatment distinct from security disputes with Beijing. Civilians do not become a collective enemy.

nodes.label: A Northern Command
nodes.description: Coordinate local reserves, field engineers and defensive positions. Prepare to defend Vietnamese core territory rather than sustaining a costly offensive mobilisation.

nodes.label: The Frontier Crisis
nodes.description: Choose a limited military purpose if a frontier crisis becomes a real war. Peaceful relations remain possible through the earlier channel.

nodes.label: Hold the Line
nodes.description: Hold prepared positions, disperse infantry under forest cover and use familiar jungle approaches. Stronger entrenchment and homeland defence come at the expense of offensive planning.

nodes.label: A Limited Counterstroke
nodes.description: Prepare a defined counteroffensive to relieve pressure or recover positions. It carries greater supply and production costs.

nodes.label: Defence in Depth
nodes.description: Organise successive defensive positions, concealed reserves and fallback lines through wooded and jungle terrain. This deepens the defence of the homeland while reducing the emphasis on offensive planning.

nodes.label: Bound the Objectives
nodes.description: Keep the counterstroke tied to a defined purpose rather than a permanent march into China. Battlefield success is never scripted.

nodes.label: Beyond the First Battle
nodes.description: Maintain the frontier after the opening invasion or counteroffensive. The main assault ending does not prove that the frontier war has ended.

nodes.label: A Soviet Commitment
nodes.description: Prepare the domestic liaison and training organization needed to seek Soviet support. The request uses existing diplomacy; it does not presume that Moscow accepts.

nodes.label: Preserve Autonomy
nodes.description: Rely more heavily on domestic resources and retain freedom of manoeuvre. Training and military output become more expensive to sustain.

nodes.label: Lessons of Assistance
nodes.description: Review an accepted Soviet mission or the limits exposed by a refusal. Preserving the military lesson does not fabricate deliveries or make Vietnam the payer of Soviet donor costs.

nodes.label: Rotate the Frontier
nodes.description: Keep formations trained for a prolonged frontier war. Rotation preserves readiness while competing with civilian recovery.

nodes.label: Account for the Fronts
nodes.description: A Cambodian commitment and a Chinese war cannot be funded as unrelated free bonuses. Define which obligation receives priority.

nodes.label: Sustain Mobilisation
nodes.description: Accept a longer exceptional commitment to preserve frontier readiness. Economic recovery is delayed.

nodes.label: A Diplomatic Opening
nodes.description: Propose a verifiable reduction of confrontation. Talks do not impose peace or claim that formal normalization has already occurred.

nodes.label: The Long Frontier
nodes.description: Prepare the army for persistent fighting and recurring strain. A larger military commitment still has to be paid for.

nodes.label: Verify the Stand down
nodes.description: Confirm accepted measures and real withdrawal before reducing the exceptional burden. No focus moves Chinese troops automatically.

nodes.label: Rebuild the North
nodes.description: Repair real damaged buildings and restore civilian life. Reconstruction requires funding and normal native construction capacity.

nodes.label: A Sustainable Frontier
nodes.description: Preserve the military lesson and a viable relationship with the neighbour. An armed frontier and negotiated coexistence remain different outcomes.

nodes.label: A Sovereign Border
nodes.description: Verify a limited border settlement without replacing the Cambodian government or inventing an occupation.

nodes.label: A Limited Commitment
nodes.description: End the exceptional military undertaking only if a limited agreement is actually fulfilled. This offers no friendly regime buffer, secured southwest dividend or military victory package.
